title: Someone Has to Let Employees Be Beginners
summary: When HR redesigns work around AI, people need room to grow into new expectations. Why letting employees be beginners belongs in the design of the job.
body_markdown:
The first time someone trusts you with work that matters, you are likely to be slower than the person who could have just done it for you.


They have to review your work. Sometimes they have to explain the same thing twice. But at some point, someone decided that helping you become capable is worth the time.


In an[earlier piece on AI work redesign](https://www.warp.co/blog/the-job-ai-didnt-replace-why-people-ops-now-has-to-design-the-work) , we discussed how People teams have to decide how jobs change around new technology. Who should teach judgment when AI takes on tasks people once learned from? People should still get a chance to grow into what the company now asks of them.


## Redesigning work has to include designing that chance to learn.


Research from[Burning Glass Institute](https://www.burningglassinstitute.org/research/the-consequence-gap?utm_source=chatgpt.com) found that, across more than a million entry-level tech job postings and practitioner interviews, employers describe seeking graduates who can “exercise judgment about work AI helps produce”.


In a recent essay for the[Thomson Reuters Institute](https://www.thomsonreuters.com/en/institute/articles/designing-judgment-reshaping-junior-senior-collaboration?utm_source=chatgpt.com) , Dorine Coffin and Lance Odegard describe a related concern: when AI supplies a junior lawyer’s starting draft, the senior colleague reviewing it may not see how the junior would have reasoned through the problem.


## Employers want the benefit of judgment, but someone has to bear the cost of developing it.


That cost includes time when a capable person is simply unfamiliar with a changed job. An experienced recruiter may be excellent at running a hiring process but still need help learning to advise a founder on the team they should build. And a manager may have to admit that they are learning alongside the person they are supposed to support.


Sure, a company can decide it only has room for experienced people. That may be a reasonable choice for a particular role or stage. But as a general answer to building a workforce, it depends on employers continuing to give people their first chances. Experience has to come from somewhere.


There is a promise inside a job well done that goes beyond the work being an exchange for a paycheck. You become someone who can do things you could not do when you arrived. You learn to trust your own assessment because you have had the chance to make one, discover its limits, and try again.


That promise matters especially when someone is ambitious. Being told you have potential is encouraging. Being trusted with a piece of consequential work, with someone available to help you through it, gives that encouragement substance.


We can absolutely retire tedious tasks while protecting the moments in which a person has to think. The work worth preserving might be a junior colleague explaining why they disagree with a recommendation, or taking responsibility for a small project before they feel entirely ready.


It can happen with AI in the room, but the person still needs a chance to arrive with a view of their own.


This requires patience from someone who is already good. It also requires a company to value what the less experienced person is becoming, even when their progress is difficult to capture in this quarter’s results.


## Asking people to change should come with room to be inexperienced again.


For People teams, this is part of the responsibility of redesigning work. If the new role depends on judgment, there needs to be a way to develop it within the job. A course can help. So can being trusted to make an assessment, then talking it through with someone who sees what you missed.


The person doing the teaching needs room to grow, too, or learning becomes something everyone endorses, and nobody has time to do.


The time saved by automating tasks with technology like AI can help create room, but that time must still be protected and built into the work redesign. Otherwise, most people simply absorb more work.


There is a real tradeoff here: the experienced person might finish the work faster, and the beginner’s progress may be difficult to capture in this quarter’s results. But a company has to decide that what someone is *becoming* deserves time alongside what they can deliver today.


Yes, they may eventually take what they learned to another company. There is generosity in helping someone become capable enough to leave you. Taking their development seriously means accepting that possibility.


Who do people get to become at your company?


HR’s work redesign decisions help determine whether that question (and promise) survives. The job needs to make room for the person who can do it well today, and for the person who is still learning how.
